profile.reading:
This building is identified in mapping data as an Amazon Web Services facility on Agnew Road in the Agnew area of Santa Clara, Santa Clara County, California, part of the long-established Silicon Valley data center market. DataCenterDynamics reported that Amazon acquired a former factory site in Santa Clara for data center use. The City of Santa Clara's own project records separately show a large data center development at 2305 Mission College Blvd, filed by an applicant named Oppidian Investment Company under city file numbers PLN2019-14213 and CEQ2020-01077, proposing to demolish an existing 358,000 square foot office and research building and replace it with two three-story data center buildings totaling approximately 490,000 square feet, plus a city substation on the site's north side; the city's own project page is marked archived and does not show a final approval or completion date. This research could not confirm with confidence that the Mission College Blvd project is the same building as this registry entry, as opposed to a separate, nearby Santa Clara facility associated with Amazon; Oppidian Investment Company, the filed applicant, is a real estate developer rather than Amazon itself, which is consistent with how hyperscale operators frequently structure data center real estate through developer or subsidiary entities rather than filing permits directly under their own corporate name.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating that this research could confirm applies specifically to this mapped Agnew Road location.

Baxtel and DataCenterMap, third-party data center listing aggregators, separately catalog an Amazon AWS facility at 960 Central Avenue in Santa Clara distinct from the Mission College Blvd address; aggregator listings are treated in this research as leads pointing to possible additional Amazon real estate in the immediate area rather than as confirmed, independently sourced facts, consistent with the general rule that directory and aggregator sites are not treated as primary sources for this page.

profile.regional_context: Santa Clara and the broader Silicon Valley corridor form one of the oldest commercial data center markets in the United States, hosting dozens of facilities from many colocation and cloud operators, including Digital Realty, Equinix, CoreSite, and Switch, in addition to Amazon and other hyperscalers. Silicon Valley Power, the City of Santa Clara's municipal electric utility, serves much of the city's data center load, and the city has separately weighed grid capacity constraints against new data center development in its own planning documents. Land in Santa Clara is largely built out, so new data center projects in the city frequently take the form of redevelopment of existing office, laboratory, or light industrial buildings, as in the Mission College Blvd project referenced above, rather than greenfield construction of the kind seen in Virginia, Ohio, or Oregon.

reading.body:
AWS has mapped a facility on Agnew Road in Santa Clara, but the operator has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or power rating for this specific location. City of Santa Clara project records show a separate large data center development at 2305 Mission College Blvd, filed under a developer entity, proposing approximately 490,000 square feet across two buildings, but this research could not confirm whether that project corresponds to the Agnew Road coordinate. Santa Clara sits in Silicon Valley, one of the oldest commercial data center markets in the United States, where new projects typically redevelop existing office or industrial buildings rather than greenfield sites, constrained by both land availability and municipal grid capacity.

Because AWS has not disclosed power capacity for this facility, its contribution to Silicon Valley's AI infrastructure cannot be quantified from published sources. The City of Santa Clara's municipal utility, Silicon Valley Power, manages grid access for the region's data center load and has raised capacity constraints in planning documents, making grid availability rather than real estate the binding factor for new development in this area.

This mapped location ranks 12th among California's published-capacity facilities but contributes zero to the state's disclosed 365 megawatts, since the operator has not published a figure. California has 103 mapped data centers but only 11 with disclosed power ratings, making this facility representative of the vast majority: real estate identified but power opaque to public analysis.
